title: Re-reading lies to you
teaser: Students who practised recalling a passage remembered 61% a week later. Students who re-read it remembered 40%, and felt more confident.

slides.alt: Cover: Re-reading lies to you. It feels like learning. A week later, the people who tested themselves remembered far more.
The experiment: students read a short science passage. Group one read it once, then wrote down what they remembered, three times. Group two just kept re-reading it.
The twist: the re-readers felt more confident they would remember it.
Bar chart: one week later, the group that wrote down what they remembered recalled 61% of the passage; the re-read group recalled 40%. Source: Roediger and Karpicke, 2006, Experiment 2.
The re-readers had read the passage about 14 times on average; the recall group about 3.4 times. Less reading, more remembering.
Try it tonight: close the book, write down everything you remember, then open it and check what you missed. Retrieval feels harder; that's why it works.
For teachers and designers: build quick, low-stakes recall into every lesson, not just a test at the end.

body: Re-reading feels like learning. It mostly isn't.

In a well-known experiment, students who read a passage once and then practised recalling it remembered 61% of it a week later. Students who simply re-read it, about 14 times in total, remembered 40%. And the re-readers were the more confident group.
The effort of pulling something out of memory is what makes it stick. Close the book, write down what you remember, then check what you missed.
forDesigners: Build quick, low-stakes recall into every lesson, not just a test at the end.

sources.label: Roediger, H.L. & Karpicke, J.D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science, 17(3), 249–255.
